newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy markets struggle to gain from rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy markets struggle to gain from rate cut.

text.p: Italian financial markets showed a muted reaction on Thursday to a surprise Bank of Italy interest rate cut late on Wednesday, economists and dealers said.
Bonds and shares rose in early business as the rate move came a month earlier than most market analysts had expected.

But comments by leading members of the Bundesbank that German interest rates were already at suitable levels, a view that all the good news was already in the market and low liquidity in shares prompted later weakness.
The lira weakened but then regained some lost ground.

The Bank of Italy moved late on Wednesday to cut its key discount rate to 7.50 percent from 8.25 percent, its first reduction since July. Some economists still see room for a further cut later this year or early next year.
Italian domestic BTP bonds rose in early trading but then drifted off with the December contract on London's LIFFE futures market slipping three basis points to 123.45.
After a firm early start, the Mibtel share index in Milan had drifted off 0.51 percent to 9,839 by 1215 GMT.
"The market's reaction to the cut was disappointing but the rate cut had been discounted in the market at some point," said Italy economist Richard Prior at HSBC.
The interest rate move took financial markets by surprise as most had believed the central bank would only cut rates in November when inflation was clearly below three percent.
The government received a further boost on Wednesday when it won a vote of confidence which it called to ram through a rescue plan for the ailing southern bank, Banco di Napoli.

Preliminary Italian consumer price inflation data published early this week showed October inflation pointing towards three percent, a threshold that the Bank of Italy had highlighted as a prelude to cutting official interest rates.

Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio has said he would want to be sure that inflation was sustainable below three percent before cutting rates. Economists had expected Fazio to make his move in November when inflation is set to dip below the three percent level.
Economists at Italy's largest bank, San Paolo, believe that inflation will slow to 2.8/2.9 percent in November and there could be a further rate cut by end-1996 of 50 basic points.
HSBC's Prior noted that the interest rate cut came on the same day that Bundesbank board member Otmar Issing said that there was no reason to expect further cuts in German rates.

The rate move and Issing's comments helped push the lira lower and a softer dollar also weighed on the Italian currency, which slipped to 1,007.80 to the mark from around 1,003 before the reduction. It later revived to 1,005.35 in mid-afternoon.

Bond dealers said that after such a strong rally over recent weeks, BTP bonds were vulnerable to profit-taking now all the good news was in the market, while there was no support for German bunds, which suffered after Issing's comments.

The early rise in Italian stocks soon faded out. Many investors kept a cautious eye out for Wall Street, which fell overnight, and Milan's perennial lack of liquidity, made worse by an offering this week of shares in energy giant ENI.
"The rate cut is a definite positive but the liquidity issue is weighing on the market," said equity market strategist Francesco Ricciulli at Milan brokerage Pasfin.

ENI is offering 8.75 percent of its stock to the market or 10 percent if a "green shoe" over-allotment for institutional buyers is included. But the Treasury said late Wednesday it would substantially increase its offer to the public due to heavy demand.

Dealers said that international investors were probably selling Italian stocks to make room in their portfolios for ENI shares as they did not want to increase their overall weighing in Italian equities.
